TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Historical Importance-Based Compression Schemes
PROPOSAL: We compare the performance of two historical importance-based compression schemes on the pre-trained T5 model: a simple scheme that keeps tokens with accumulated attention scores > 0.5, and a complex scheme that uses a learned model to predict token importance. The experiments use the "Long-Context" version of the NewsQA dataset, consisting of 100,000+ tokens. Our primary metric is the accuracy drop on the evaluation set when initializing all key-value cache positions with the compressed representation.
CONTROLS: An ablation that evaluates the efficacy of the learned model, as well as a baseline where the key-value cache is not compressed.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (small batches for extensive evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect the complex scheme to outperform the simple one by 10% in terms of accuracy drop, whereas the baseline may exhibit a 30% drop.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of KV Cache Size on Compression Schemes
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the strictness of the historical importance threshold on KV cache compression in the T5 model. By dynamically varying the cache size and comparing the performance at different compression levels, we aim to identify the optimal historical importance threshold as a function of available memory (i.e., KV cache size).
CONTROLS: Experimental proposal 1 with multiple historical importance thresholds (e.g., 0.25, 0.5, 0.75), as well as a baseline where no compression is employed.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (fixed batch size across multiple runs)
PREDICTION: We expect to find a threshold-linear relationship, where a higher cache size requires a lower importance threshold to maintain similar model performance, and vice versa. Moreover, the simple scheme (threshold 0.5) may perform significantly better than the complex scheme when KV cache size is limited.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Exploring the Role of Contextualized Token Importance
PROPOSAL: We modify historical importance-based caching to utilize contextualized token embeddings (e.g., learned in the BERT model) to attribute importance values to each token. By examining the robustness of contextual importance attributions under different masking patterns, we can infer whether the information represented by contextualized token importance complements or replaces standard attention-based attributions.
CONTROLS: A basic version of proposal 1 (non-contextualized importance), as well as a baseline with no attention bias correction.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (cross-validation setup for understanding masking pattern stability)
PREDICTION: We expect a moderate improvement (around 8%) compared to baseline 1 when contextualizing importance attributions, indicating that contextualized token embeddings bring valuable features to the importance scoring task.

TITLE: Investigating KV Cache Redundancies in Long-Context LLMs
PROPOSAL: This experiment aims to identify the characteristics of LLM attention patterns that lead to local redundancy in the KV cache. We will analyze the attention weights and KV cache entries of a pre-trained large LLM on long-document question answering and document summarization tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results with a baseline that randomly discards KV cache entries to simulate hard pruning. Additionally, we will analyze the attention weights and cache entries for different context lengths to understand how redundancy changes as context length increases.

PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will compare the performance of different cache merging schemes, including Hierarchical Clustering, DBSCAN, and k-means, on a range of long-context LLMs and tasks, including long-document question answering and code completion. We will evaluate the quality of the merged representations using metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score on a held-out validation set.

COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (training and evaluation of different merging schemes on 5 LLMs and 10 tasks)
PREDICTION: We expect the Hierarchical Clustering and DBSCAN methods to perform better than the simple k-nearest neighbors approach, especially on tasks with longer contexts, but the performance difference may vary based on the quality of attention patterns. Regions of ambiguity may appear for codes where the context chunks have overlapping entity granularity.
